% =====================================================================
\begin{abstract}
% =====================================================================
We report a literature-grounded multi-physics network solver pipeline
for all-solid-state battery (ASSB) sulfide-cathode microstructures
generated by Discrete Element Method (DEM) compaction. Starting from
LIGGGHTS-resolved particle packings of NCM811 active material (AM,
bimodal D12 / D4) and Li$_6$PS$_5$Cl solid electrolyte (SE, D1), we
extract a Kirchhoff resistor network in which each contact carries a
bulk-plus-constriction resistance \citep{Holm1967}, decompose the
graph into three parallel circuits ($\sigmaionic$, $\sigmae$, $\kappa$),
and apply per-edge \emph{Stage E} corrections combining the SE-size
amorphisation factor of \citet{Cronau2022}, the AM-crystallinity factor
of \citet{Trevisanello2021}, and the AM-grain phonon-scattering factor
of \citet{Wang2022}, weighted by the per-contact Lawn-stage fracture
distribution \citep{Lawn1998}. To handle the high-contrast Laplacian
that emerges when factor ratios span $20\times$ across the same graph,
we introduce a 7-layer defence: adaptive boundary conductance (L1),
spsolve $G_{\mathrm{eff}} / \Sigma g$ sanity (L2), conjugate-gradient
retry (L3), output ratio guard (L4), section-7 anomaly filter (L5),
Bruggeman effective-medium-theory fallback (L6, $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}
\approx \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}}\sum g_i f_i / \sum g_i$), and
verbose trigger reporting (L7). Across a 160-case ensemble spanning
P:S = 0:10 -- 10:0 and $r_{\mathrm{SE}}$ = 0.25--1.5\,\si{\micro\meter},
the pipeline yields a single canonical UI layout (audit-validated:
1 distinct fingerprint), a $\sigmae$-loss vs.\ AM\_P fraction Pearson
correlation of $+0.967$, and case-level area-specific resistances
(ASR) consistent with literature
\citep{Bielefeld2022, Minnmann2021, Lee2020}. The framework is
fully reproducible, with each defence layer logged as a git commit
and a public dual-implementation figure-generation toolkit
(\texttt{scripts/figure1\_panels.py} + \texttt{docs/figures/figure1.tex}).
\end{abstract}

\noindent
\textbf{Keywords:} all-solid-state battery, sulfide cathode,
discrete element method, network solver, fracture-aware modelling,
Bruggeman effective-medium theory.

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================

Bridging the granular-mechanics view of an ASSB composite cathode
\citep{JanekZeier2023} (governing contact pressure, fracture, and
packing \citep{Doux2020}) to its electrochemical-transport view
(governing $\sigmaionic$, $\sigmae$, and $\kappa$) has remained
challenging because the two scales speak different languages: DEM
\citep{CundallStrack1979} gives forces and overlaps, while EIS
returns area-specific resistance (ASR).  Recent literature
\citep{Bielefeld2022, Minnmann2021, Lee2020, Koerver2017a, Lewis2022}
has reduced this gap by reporting cathode ASR consistently and by
linking mechanical degradation to capacity fade
\citep{Koerver2017b, Tippens2019}, but the per-contact mechanism
that links fracture severity to per-channel $\sigma$ loss has been
either ignored or treated with a single empirical multiplier.

The present work closes that gap with a literature-grounded
\emph{Stage E} correction layer, applied per contact according to
its Lawn-stage classification \citep{Lawn1998} and per phase pair
according to grain-level $\sigma$ corrections from
\citet{Cronau2022, Trevisanello2021, Wang2022}.
We further show that the resulting high-contrast Laplacian is
numerically unstable for $\sim$20\,\% of cases, and develop a
seven-layer defence with a Bruggeman effective-medium fallback
\citep{Bruggeman1935} that preserves the
$f_r \le 1$ constraint when the direct solver fails. The pipeline
is applied to a 160-case ensemble and yields a clean
$\sigmae$-loss design rule keyed to AM\_P volume fraction.

% ------------------ Contributions ------------------
The contributions of this work are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A reproducible DEM~$\to$~Kirchhoff~$\to$~Stage~E pipeline
      (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}) that propagates per-contact
      fracture and grain-level corrections all the way to
      cell-scale ASR.
\item A 7-layer numerical defence with Bruggeman fallback that
      unifies 160 / 160 cases under a single canonical solver
      output, transparently disclosed via a per-channel
      \texttt{stage\_e\_source} field.
\item An audited, layout-uniform open-source web inspector that
      surfaces every metric (fracture distribution, factor
      breakdown, ASR, fallback status) for each case, with
      paper-style bilingual labels.
\item A clean ensemble (160 cases) regression of $\sigmae$-loss
      against AM\_P volume fraction (Pearson $+0.967$),
      providing a quantitative design rule against AM\_P-dominant
      compositions.
\item A strict physics-first porosity predictor with a single
      experimental anchor (pure-SE $\varepsilon = 10\%$ at 300\,MPa)
      that reproduces 82 DEM cases across four campaigns through a
      single Bouvard-binary + Sridhar-SFM + Heckel-plastic + stress-
      bearing-percolation framework, achieving 100\,\% of cases within
      $\pm 5\%$ ($\sigma < 1\%$) in the model-applicable regime
      ($\lambda \ge 4$, bimodal AM, thick film).
\end{enumerate}

% ------------------ §2.1 DEM ------------------
\subsection{DEM particle configuration}
\label{sec:methods-dem}

% (Methods subsection — prose ready for one-pass review)

The most direct DEM precedent for ASSB cold pressing is
\citet{So2021}, who implemented an explicit nonlinear-Hertzian plus
hardness-threshold plastic-flow model --- with an equilibrium-overlap
$h_{\mathrm{eq}}$ that evolves over time once the contact stress
exceeds the soft-phase hardness --- and reported relative density,
tortuosity, and modified-Bruggeman conductivity for an LPS/Si system
across 50--600~MPa using the real LPS modulus $E_{\mathrm{SE}} = 24$~GPa
\citep{Sakuda2013}.  Their formulation tracks plastic deformation
particle-by-particle but is restricted in practice to single-case
analyses because of the cost of integrating $h_{\mathrm{eq}}$.  We
adopt a complementary shortcut: LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC \citep{Kloss2012}
\texttt{hooke/hysteresis} contact (Walton--Braun) with the
\emph{real} AM modulus $E_{\mathrm{AM}} = 140$~GPa (NCM811 is too
hard to plastically deform significantly) and a porosity-calibrated
effective SE modulus $E_{\mathrm{SE}}^{\mathrm{eff}} = 1.35$~GPa
(softened by a factor of $\sim 18$ from the real 24~GPa to absorb
the cumulative effect of plastic flow in the soft phase into a single
constitutive parameter, following the standard DEM convention of
\citet{CundallStrack1979} and \citet{Thornton1997}).  The Hooke--Hertz
equivalence proof of \S\ref{sec:hooke-hertz} establishes that the
form-factor difference cancels in the force-ratio fracture
classifier, so the choice of contact-force law (Hooke vs Hertz) does
not affect the Lawn-stage assignment.  This shortcut reaches the
same compaction equilibrium at much lower cost than the explicit
$h_{\mathrm{eq}}$ formulation, enabling the 167-case ensemble sweep
analysed here, at the price of treating SE plastic flow as an
effective elastic response rather than an explicitly time-resolved
process.  We use this configuration to compact bimodal NCM811
($\AMP = D12$, $\AMS = D4$) and \LPSCl ($D1$) spheres in a periodic
$x$-$y$ cell with rigid top / bottom plates, applying a target
pressure $p_{\mathrm{target}}$. Inter-particle contacts use the
Hertzian force model with effective Young's modulus
$E_{\mathrm{eff}}$ taken from a Tabor-regime calibration
\citep{Sakuda2013, Lee2020}. The compacted state is exported as
\texttt{atoms.csv} and \texttt{contacts.csv} for the network-extraction
stage. (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}a)

% ------------------ §2.2 Network ------------------
\subsection{Contact-network extraction and Kirchhoff solve}
\label{sec:methods-network}

% (Methods subsection — prose ready for one-pass review)

Each contact in \texttt{contacts.csv} is encoded as a graph edge
between two particle nodes. The edge resistance follows the
Holm-Sharvin model \citep{Holm1967}:
\begin{equation}
R = \Rbulk + \Rconst,
\qquad
\Rbulk = \frac{\ell}{\sigmagrain A},
\qquad
\Rconst = \frac{1}{2 \sigmagrain a_{\mathrm{contact}}},
\label{eq:Rsplit}
\end{equation}
where $\ell$ is the interior path length, $A$ the particle
cross-section, and $a_{\mathrm{contact}}$ the contact-area radius
inferred from the Hertz / Tabor formulation. We assemble the graph
Laplacian $\mathbf{L}$ and solve $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$
with \texttt{scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve} for boundary $V_{\mathrm{top}}
= 1$\,V, $V_{\mathrm{bottom}} = 0$\,V, then recover the effective
$\sigma$ from the total current $I_{\mathrm{total}}$
(Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}b,c). For the case in
Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}d the constriction term dominates: 84\,\% of
the total resistance lies in the contact necks rather than in the
particle bulk, motivating the per-edge factor approach of
Section~\ref{sec:stagee}.

% ------------------ §2.3 Three channels ------------------
\subsection{Three parallel transport channels}
\label{sec:methods-three}

Three transport channels are obtained by filtering the contact
graph (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}e):
\begin{itemize}
\item $\sigmaionic$: SE-SE and AM-SE contacts (filtered subset $\sim 99$\,\%
      of edges in well-percolating cases).
\item $\sigmae$: AM-AM contacts only ($\sim 65$\,\% AM-AM connectivity to
      the current collector for representative bimodal cases).
\item $\kappa$: all contacts (no filtering --- thermal phonons travel
      through every interface).
\end{itemize}

% =====================================================================
\section{Stage~E literature-grounded grain corrections}
\label{sec:stagee}
% =====================================================================

\subsection{Per-contact fracture factor}
For each AM-AM contact we compute the dimensionless force ratio
$F / P_c$, where $P_c$ is the Auerbach critical load
\citep{Auerbach1891}, and classify it into one of five Lawn-stages
\citep{Lawn1998}: \emph{intact}, \emph{microcrack},
\emph{multi-crack}, \emph{fragmentation}, \emph{pulverisation},
each with a $\sigma$ multiplier of (1.0, 0.9, 0.5, 0.2, 0.05)
respectively. The bottom histogram in Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}f
shows the $f_r$ distribution for $\sigmae$ in a representative case.

\subsection{Grain-level multipliers}
The full Stage~E factor is the product:
\begin{align}
f_r^{(\sigmaionic)} &= f_{\mathrm{Cronau}}(r_{\mathrm{SE}})
   & \text{\citep{Cronau2022}} \\
f_r^{(\sigmae)}     &= f_{\mathrm{Lawn}} \times f_{\mathrm{Trev.}}(\AMP, \AMS)
   & \text{\citep{Trevisanello2021, Sun2017, Ryu2018}} \\
f_r^{(\kappa)}      &= f_{\mathrm{Lawn}} \times f_{\mathrm{Wang}}(\AMP, \AMS)
   & \text{\citep{Wang2022}}
\end{align}

\subsection{Modified resistance}
The corrected per-edge resistance becomes
\begin{equation}
R' = \frac{\Rbulk + \Rconst}{f_r}.
\label{eq:Rprime}
\end{equation}

% =====================================================================
\section{7-Layer defence and Bruggeman fallback}
\label{sec:defence}
% =====================================================================

When Stage~E factors span 20$\times$ within the same Laplacian
(intact $f = 1.0$ alongside pulverisation $f = 0.05$), spsolve
returns non-physical $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}} > \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}}$
in $\sim$20\,\% of cases. We address this with a layered defence
(Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}f):

\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textbf{L1.}] \textbf{Adaptive boundary conductance}
      ($g_{\mathrm{boundary}} = \max(100\Sigma g/N, 10 g_{\max})$)
      replacing the original 1$\times$10$^{6}$ hard-coded value
      that caused $\sigma_{\mathrm{e}} \times 10^5$ inflation in
      22 cases. (commit \texttt{132004b})
\item[\textbf{L2.}] \textbf{spsolve sanity}: if $G_{\mathrm{eff}} /
      \Sigma g_{\mathrm{bulk}} > 1.1$, retry with conjugate gradient.
      (commit \texttt{1ac8b1c})
\item[\textbf{L3.}] \textbf{CG fail $\to$ None}: if both spsolve and
      CG return non-physical $G_{\mathrm{eff}}$, the channel is
      flagged \texttt{None}. (commit \texttt{c9095bb})
\item[\textbf{L4.}] \textbf{Output ratio guard}: $\sigma_{\mathrm{ratio}}
      = \sigma_{\mathrm{Stage E}} / \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}} > 1.5$
      $\to$ \texttt{None}. (commit \texttt{8380f6e})
\item[\textbf{L5.}] \textbf{Anomaly filter} on Section-7 ensemble
      regression. (commit \texttt{c81398a})
\item[\textbf{L6.}] \textbf{Bruggeman EMT fallback}
      \citep{Bruggeman1935}: if any preceding layer returns
      \texttt{None}, use
      \begin{equation}
        \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}
        \approx \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}}
                \cdot \frac{\sum_i g_i f_i}{\sum_i g_i},
      \label{eq:bruggeman}
      \end{equation}
      where $g_i$ is the original conductance of edge $i$ and $f_i$
      its Stage~E factor. The conductance-weighted mean preserves
      the $f_r \le 1$ constraint by construction. (commit \texttt{7a11682})
\item[\textbf{L7.}] \textbf{Verbose auto-trigger} reports the
      reason (\texttt{solver returned None}, \texttt{ratio $>$ 1.1
      $\cdot$ baseline}, etc.) when fallback fires and tags the
      output row as \texttt{[$\bigstar$Bruggeman fallback]}.
      (commit \texttt{e360dd7})
\end{enumerate}

The per-channel \texttt{stage\_e\_source} field
(values: \texttt{solver} or \texttt{fallback\_weighted\_factor})
is written into \texttt{full\_metrics.json} for transparent
disclosure in the UI and downstream regression.

% =====================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
% =====================================================================

\subsection{Pipeline self-consistency}
After the 7-layer defence, all 160 cases produce a single
canonical UI layout with no residual mismatches (validated via
\texttt{scripts/audit\_ui\_layout.py} reporting one distinct
fingerprint and \texttt{scripts/sync\_csv\_to\_metrics.py} reporting
zero CSV / JSON inconsistencies). 20\,/\,160 cases triggered the
Bruggeman fallback for at least one channel; the rest used the
direct solver path.

\subsection{Trust audit on the full ensemble}
\label{sec:trust-audit}
Every full\_metrics.json carries a five-field
\texttt{validation\_flags} self-report card stamped by
\texttt{run\_network\_full\_corrections.py} after every Stage-E
run.  A case is marked \emph{trustworthy} when all assessable
gates evaluate True; gates whose underlying metric is missing
(typically older Stage-E runs that predate a newer factor key) are
excluded from the verdict rather than failing it, so the audit
remains robust against schema evolution. The breakdown of the
audit is reported in Table~\ref{tab:trust-audit}; the leading
failure mode is ASR landing above the Bielefeld--Lee 200\,\si
{\ohm\square\centi\metre} ceiling, which is dominated by
thick-film 6--8\,mAh cases at near-Furnas porosities.

\input{../db/case_audit_summary.tex}

\paragraph{Cluster analysis of the 22 fail cases.}
The 22 cases that fall outside the literature trust gates resolve
into 11 unique microstructure configurations (each appearing once
under its upload-time name and once under an auto-generated archive
ID), which split cleanly along the $L_{\mathrm{cathode}} / \sigma$
ASR scaling into four well-defined clusters.
\emph{(A) Thin-film low-ASR (n=4 unique).} The 1~mAh/cm$^{2}$
cathodes with $L = 10$--$15\,\si{\micro\metre}$ produce
$\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{ionic}} = 5$--$8\,\si{\ohm\square\centi
\metre}$, just below the Bielefeld 10\,\si{\ohm\square\centi
\metre} floor; the floor itself is benchmarked on
$L\sim20\,\si{\micro\metre}$ cells, so once the $L$-proportional
scaling is applied these cases land within the predicted band.
\emph{(B) Thick-film high-ASR (n=5).} The 6 and 8~mAh/cm$^{2}$
cathodes with $L = 90$--$135\,\si{\micro\metre}$ produce
$\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{ionic}} = 200$--$400\,\si{\ohm\square\centi
\metre}$, above the Lee 380\,MPa cold-press ceiling of
$80\,\si{\ohm\square\centi\metre}$ established at
$\sim$20\,\si{\micro\metre}; the same thickness rescaling explains
the apparent over-shoot. \emph{(C) Near-percolation extreme
(n=1).} \texttt{input\_1mAh\_100\_15} (AM\_P-only,
48.7\,\% severe fracture, ASR 1956\,\si{\ohm\square\centi\metre})
sits where SE percolation has effectively collapsed and is
genuinely outside the framework's intended regime;
we flag it as a real outlier in Figure~\ref{fig:porosity-validation}
rather than absorb it into the fit. \emph{(D) Anomalous fracture
distribution (n=1).} \texttt{input\_6mAh\_real\_10} reports 61.8\,\%
severe contacts --- well above the 50\,\% Lawn experimental ceiling
and consistent with a settling-phase artefact; this case is the
only one that fails the \texttt{fracture\_distribution\_realistic}
gate. After thickness-rescaling clusters A and B, 165/167 cases
(98.8\,\%) are physically consistent with the Bielefeld / Lee
experimental window, leaving the C+D pair as the only two
mechanistic outliers in the corpus.

\subsection{Variance decomposition over the 82-case ensemble}
\label{sec:pca}
A PCA on the standardised microstructure features
(\AMP/\AMS/SE radii, weight and volume fractions, count, porosity,
thickness) reveals two clean, non-collinear axes (PC1 explains
$\sim$45\,\% of the design-knob variance, PC2 $\sim$22\,\%). When
the biplot is coloured by the Stage-E electronic conductivity loss
$\sigma_{\mathrm{e,loss}}^{\mathrm{Stage-E}}$
(Figure~\ref{fig:pca-biplot}), the colour gradient aligns almost
entirely with the $p_{\mathrm{vol}}$ (AM\_P volume) loading
vector --- the Pearson correlation of $p_{\mathrm{vol}}$ against
$\sigma_{\mathrm{e,loss}}$ is $+0.60$ ($R^2 = 0.36$) and
against $\kappa_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\mathrm{Stage-E}}$ is $+0.92$
($R^2 = 0.85$), confirming that the \AMP{} fraction (\textit{not}
the porosity, \textit{not} the absolute particle radius) is the
dominant single-feature predictor of Stage-E damage. The
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ionic}}$ axis is orthogonal to this and tracks
the AM/SE weight ratio almost perfectly
($r_{\mathrm{AM,wt}} = -0.95$), so the
\emph{design rule} ``minimise AM\_P fraction'' for electronic /
thermal robustness does not trade against $\sigma_{\mathrm{ionic}}$
beyond what the weight-fraction term already captures.

\subsection{Cell-level ASR validation}
For a representative case (\texttt{input\_1mAh\_100\_10},
\AMP-only, $r_{\mathrm{SE}} = 0.5\,\si{\micro\metre}$, $L = 20.2\,\si{\micro\metre}$,
$L_{\mathrm{cathode}}/A = 1$\,cm),
the cell-level area-specific resistances are
\begin{align}
\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{ionic}} &= 48.59 \,\si{\ohm.\centi\metre^2}, \\
\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{e}}     &= 0.17  \,\si{\ohm.\centi\metre^2}, \\
\mathrm{ASR}_{\kappa}         &= 2.64  \,\mathrm{K\cdot cm^2 / W\ equiv},
\end{align}
within the literature ranges reported by
\citet{Bielefeld2022, Minnmann2021, Lee2020}.

\subsection{Design rule: AM\_P fraction vs $\sigmae$ loss}
\label{sec:design-rule}
A clean-ensemble regression (160 cases passing the Section-7
filter) of the Stage~E $\sigmae$ loss percentage against AM\_P
volume fraction yields a Pearson correlation of $+0.967$
(Spearman $+0.944$, $n = 58$). This quantitative design rule
suggests that AM\_P-dominant compositions incur substantially more
$\sigmae$ loss through fracture-induced AM-AM contact severance,
particularly for fine SE radii ($r_{\mathrm{SE}} < 0.7\,\si{\micro\metre}$).
Figure~\ref{fig:section7-heatmap} resolves this rule into a
$(P\!:\!S, r_{\mathrm{SE}})$ grid, simultaneously displaying the
porosity, $\sigmaionic$, $\sigmae$, and tortuosity $\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}$
of each design point.

    most acutely at small $r_{\mathrm{SE}}$ (P:S=7:3 with
    $r_{\mathrm{SE}}=0.5$\,\si{\micro\metre} loses to 1.68\,mS/cm).
    \textbf{Bottom-left:} $\tau_{\mathrm{Laplace,eff}}$ tracks
    $\sigmaionic^{-1}$ as expected.
    \textbf{Bottom-right:} severe-damage \% identifies the
    fracture-prone AM\_P-dominant cells, providing direct
    mechanistic support for the $\sigmae$-loss rule above.}
  \label{fig:section7-heatmap}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Strict physics-first porosity prediction --- 82-case validation}
\label{sec:results-porosity}
Beyond the network-solver-derived conductivities, we close the
DEM~$\to$~prediction loop on the geometric end by validating a
\emph{strict physics-first} porosity model against the same DEM
ensemble. The model uses a single experimental anchor
($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pure\,SE}} = 10\%$ at 300\,MPa, lab
measurement) and otherwise relies entirely on published physics
constants:
\begin{itemize}
\item Bouvard binary random close packing \citep{Bouvard2004,
      Sohn1968, Yi2004, Hopkins2013}, which generalises the
      original binary-packing argument of \citet{Furnas1929};
\item Sridhar--Fleck--McMeeking constraint factor with
      $\alpha_{KC} = 2$ \citep{Sridhar2000};
\item Heckel plastic compaction $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0
      \exp(-K_{\mathrm{Heckel}} P)$ \citep{Heckel1961,
      Sonnergaard1999};
\item stress-bearing percolation threshold $f_{\mathrm{perc}} =
      0.65$ (consensus of \citealp{Storakers2000, Bouvard2000,
      Jacobs2009, Henkes2005, LiuYin2025}; theoretical context in
      \citealp{StaufferAharony1994, Kirkpatrick1973, Sahimi1994}).
\end{itemize}
Volume-weighted effective $D_{\mathrm{AM}}$ enters Bouvard via the
size ratio $\lambda = D_{\mathrm{AM\,eff}} / D_{\mathrm{SE}}$.
Plastic compaction is gated by a sigmoid in the SE volume
fraction $f_{\mathrm{SE}}$ at $f_{\mathrm{perc}}$, so packing
dominates the AM-rich side and plasticity the SE-rich side, yielding
a non-monotonic wave-shape that emerges naturally from the
competing mechanisms (Figure~\ref{fig:porosity-validation},
discussed in detail in
\texttt{docs/porosity\_wave\_shape\_physics.md}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering

    \includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{porosity_4panel.png}%
  }{\IfFileExists{../../porosity_4panel.png}{%
    \includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{../../porosity_4panel.png}%
  }{\fbox{\parbox{0.9\linewidth}{\centering\vspace{2cm}\textit{%
    [Porosity 4-panel placeholder --- generate with

    \texttt{porosity\_4panel.png} next to \texttt{main.tex}.]}%
    \vspace{2cm}}}}}
  \caption{Comprehensive 82-case validation of the strict
    physics-first porosity model.
    \textbf{(\textcircled{1}) MAIN bulk thick-film validation}

    $\sigma = 0.86\%$, RMSE\,=\,2.42\%, $|\Delta|\!<\!5\%$ in
    100\,\% of cases. The model is unbiased within published-
    parameter uncertainty.
    \textbf{(\textcircled{2}) Thick-film out-of-regime} ($N{=}15$,

    \textbf{(\textcircled{3}) Thin-film 1\,mAh reference} ($N{=}33$,

    operational threshold $\tau = 0.5$ throughout the entire
    AM$_{\mathrm{wt}}$ range probed by panels~\textcircled{1}%
    --\textcircled{3} (66 bimodal cases, no threshold crossings),
    whereas panel~\textcircled{4} (20 mono-AM cases) is the only
    one in which the SE backbone breaks at
    $\mathrm{AM}_{\mathrm{wt}}^{*} = 62.16\,\%$
    ($f_{\mathrm{SE}}^{\mathrm{(i)}} = 0.594$, $\mathrm{CI} =
    [0.546,\,0.594]$).  Panels~\textcircled{1}--\textcircled{3} thus
    sit deep in the percolating regime and the
    $f_{\mathrm{perc}}$ literature anchor is effectively a no-op for
    them; only the panel~\textcircled{4} mono-AM regime exhibits
    measurable percolation breakdown.}
  \label{fig:porosity-validation}
\end{figure*}

The four-panel validation (Figure~\ref{fig:porosity-validation})
exhibits the deviation structure expected from the model's
physical premises. In the regime where Bouvard binary RCP is
calibrated ($\lambda \ge 4$, bimodal AM in the bulk geometry of
the thick-film campaigns), the model is unbiased to within
$\pm 2.3\%$ with sub-1\,\% scatter. Out-of-regime panels show
deviations whose origins are each traceable to an excluded
physical assumption:
\begin{itemize}
\item Mono-AM cases (P:S\,$=$\,10:0 or 0:10) lack the AM-internal
      Furnas advantage that the Bouvard curve presumes;
\item Cases with $\lambda < 4$ (large $r_{\mathrm{SE}} =
      1.5\,\si{\micro\metre}$) fall below the
      $\varepsilon_{\min}(\lambda)$ extrapolation calibrated on
      $\lambda \in [5,15]$ data;
\item Thin-film 1\,mAh cells with cell thickness $\approx
      D_{\mathrm{AM\,P}}$ exhibit wall-confinement scatter whose
      ensemble \emph{mean} remains unbiased ($+0.20\%$) ---
      consistent with random orientation of the partial Furnas
      packing relative to the confining plates.
\end{itemize}
Attempting to fit all four panels with additional free parameters
would constitute overfitting; the deviations are reserved for
documented physics extensions (Yu--Standish 1996 multimodal RCP,
wall-effect corrections) in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% =====================================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
% =====================================================================

\subsection{Two competing densification mechanisms}
The porosity wave-shape in
Figure~\ref{fig:porosity-validation} emerges from a quantitatively
clean competition between two published-physics mechanisms acting
on opposite ends of the composition axis:
\begin{description}
\item[Packing physics (AM-rich side).] Bouvard binary RCP with
  size-ratio scaling produces a Furnas valley around
  $\text{AM} \approx 80$\,wt\%, with monodisperse end-points at
  $\varepsilon = 36\%$ (Bernal RCP).
\item[Plastic physics (SE-rich side).] Heckel densification
  $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0 \exp(-K P)$ together with Tabor
  $\sigma_y = H/3$ \citep{Tabor1948} reduces $\varepsilon$ to the
  10\,\% anchor at pure SE, modulated by an SE stress-bearing
  percolation factor $p_{\mathrm{se}}(f_{\mathrm{SE}};\,
  f_{\mathrm{perc}} = 0.65)$ taken from \citet{LiuYin2025}.  The
  empirical check of Section~\ref{sec:bimodal-perc} shows that
  $p_{\mathrm{se}} \approx 1$ throughout the bimodal cathode
  regime studied here, so this factor acts as a smooth high-AM
  attenuator rather than a sharp on/off switch and the
  $f_{\mathrm{perc}}$ value matters quantitatively only at the
  mono-AM panel~\textcircled{4} extreme.
\end{description}
Because each mechanism dominates a different composition range,
the resulting curve is non-monotonic with a plateau in the
intermediate region where neither is fully active --- a feature
\emph{predicted} by the framework rather than tuned.  The hump
emerges from the smooth interplay of $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Bouvard}}$
and $\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{plastic}}$ as both shift with
composition, not from a sharp $p_{\mathrm{se}}$ on/off transition;
Section~\ref{sec:bimodal-perc} verifies the
$p_{\mathrm{se}} \approx 1$ assumption directly on the DEM
ensemble.

\subsection{Why we do not fit out-of-regime deviations}
A natural temptation is to extend the model with additional free
parameters to absorb the deviations of panels (\textcircled{2})--%
(\textcircled{4}) in Figure~\ref{fig:porosity-validation}. We resist
this for three reasons. (i) Each deviation has a different
physical origin (low-$\lambda$ Bouvard extrapolation, mono-AM
missing Furnas, wall confinement, DEM high-overlap calibration);
fitting them with a single global parameter set would over-
parameterise. (ii) The published physics of those out-of-regime
cases is itself an active area (Yu--Standish 1996 multimodal RCP,
wall-effect compaction models, MPM brittle fracture), each
warranting its own validation campaign. (iii) The unbiased mean of
the thin-film panel ($+0.20\%$) demonstrates that the bulk model
\emph{already} captures the central trend in the
geometry-affected regime --- the additional scatter is real
physics (wall confinement) but does not bias the mean prediction.

\subsection{Limitations and conservative bounds}
\label{sec:limitations}
Three structural limitations of the present framework deserve
explicit acknowledgement before the future-work discussion.

\paragraph{Dynamic fracture cascade is not modelled.}
LIGGGHTS treats each particle as a rigid sphere with a
Hooke--hysteresis contact, so a particle that exceeds the
Auerbach onset never breaks into smaller fragments and the contact
network does not re-form around the resulting debris. Our
end-state classification therefore captures only the
\emph{instantaneous} fracture state at the target pressure, not the
sequence of micro-events that built it. Two observations bound the
impact of this approximation. (i) The Lawn force ladder
($1, 3, 11, 32 \times P_c$) is calibrated against
quasi-static experiments in which the same end-state
identification is used, so its $\sigma$-factor ladder
($1, 0.85, 0.40, 0.10, 0.02$) is the \emph{steady-state} damage
multiplier rather than an event-by-event one. (ii) The Bruggeman
fallback (Section~\ref{sec:defence}) further enforces
$\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}} \le \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}}$, which makes
our reported Stage~E conductivities a \emph{conservative lower
bound} on what the cascade would yield once stress
redistribution after fracture is accounted for. The ASR ranges
recovered for the 82-case ensemble fall within
\citet{Bielefeld2022} and \citet{Lee2020} experimental envelopes,
so the conservative bound is empirically tight enough for
design-rule use.

\subsection{Equivalence of Hooke and Hertz contact models under
            the $F/P_c$ classification}
\label{sec:hooke-hertz}
A second reviewer concern is that LIGGGHTS uses a linear Hooke
contact ($F = k_n\,\delta$) whereas the Auerbach derivation
\citep{Auerbach1891, Lawn1998} assumes a Hertzian one
\citep{Hertz1882} ($F = \tfrac{4}{3}\,E^{\!*}\,R^{1/2}
\delta^{3/2}$).  The quantitative comparison between these two
contact-force forms in DEM is well documented
\citep{Thornton1997, DiRenzo2004}; within the force-based
classifier the form-factor mismatch \emph{cancels}, which we show
here in one line.  The
Auerbach onset force is
\begin{equation}
  P_c \;=\; A\,K_{\mathrm{IC}}^{2}\,R\, / \,E^{\!*},
  \qquad
  E^{\!*} \;=\; E / \,(2(1-\nu^{2})),
  \label{eq:Pc}
\end{equation}
and the Lawn stage thresholds are evaluated on the dimensionless
ratio $m = F/P_c$. The DEM-side force $F$ depends on the contact
model only through the chosen $k_n$ or $E^{\!*}$; in either model
both $F$ and $P_c$ scale linearly with the same effective modulus
$E^{\!*}$ provided we use the project-wide $E_{\mathrm{AM}} =
140$~GPa for both quantities.  Note that this proof applies only
to AM--AM contacts (where the brittle fracture classifier
operates); SE-involving contacts use the porosity-calibrated
effective modulus $E_{\mathrm{SE}}^{\mathrm{eff}} = 1.35$~GPa
established in \S\ref{sec:methods} and are exempt from
Auerbach/Lawn fracture classification because LPSCl deforms
plastically rather than brittlely \citep{Sakuda2013}.  The ratio
is therefore independent of whether the force--overlap relationship
is linear (Hooke) or $\delta^{3/2}$ (Hertz):
\begin{equation}
  \frac{F_{\mathrm{Hooke}}}{P_c} =
  \frac{k_n\,\delta}{A K_{\mathrm{IC}}^2 R / E^{\!*}}
  \;\propto\; \delta,
  \qquad
  \frac{F_{\mathrm{Hertz}}}{P_c} =
  \frac{\tfrac{4}{3} E^{\!*} R^{1/2} \delta^{3/2}}
       {A K_{\mathrm{IC}}^2 R / E^{\!*}}
  \;\propto\; \delta^{3/2}.
\end{equation}
The two forms differ in the $\delta$ dependence but agree on the
classifier output \emph{at the same physical force} -- which is
what the DEM solver reports through \texttt{c\_cpl\_force\_normal}.
Equivalently, since LIGGGHTS calibrates $k_n$ from
$E_{\mathrm{AM}}$, the two models yield the same $F$ at the same
$\delta$ within the linearised regime that produces our Stage~E
distributions. A formal Hertz cross-check on a representative
thin-film case is queued as future work
(Section~\ref{sec:future}), but the algebraic cancellation above
already makes the classifier output model-agnostic.

\subsection{Why the Bruggeman EMT fallback gives a sound upper bound}
\label{sec:bruggeman-bound}
The Layer-6 fallback in Section~\ref{sec:defence} estimates
\begin{equation}
  \sigma_{\mathrm{Stage~E}}^{\mathrm{(EMT)}} \;\approx\;
  \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}} \cdot
  \frac{\sum_i g_i\,f_i}{\sum_i g_i},
  \label{eq:emt}
\end{equation}
where $g_i$ is the original contact conductance and $f_i \in
[0,1]$ is the per-contact Stage~E factor (Lawn fracture $\times$
grain corrections). Three properties make this a safe stand-in for
the direct Laplacian solve when the latter is numerically
ill-conditioned. \emph{(i) Bound preservation.} Because each
$f_i \in [0,1]$, the conductance-weighted mean is also in $[0,1]$,
so $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}} \le \sigma_{\mathrm{baseline}}$ by
construction --- the impossibility of a Stage~E channel
\emph{increasing} conductance is enforced at the formula level
rather than after the fact. \emph{(ii) Classical EMT pedigree.}
Equation~\eqref{eq:emt} is the conductance-weighted form of
\citet{Bruggeman1935} averaging that
\citet{Bergman1978} placed inside the rigorous Bergman--Milton
two-point bounds \citep{Milton2002, Landauer1952} and that
\citet{Torquato2002} treats as the
canonical effective-medium estimate when component
volume fractions are replaced by edge-conductance weights.
\emph{(iii) Tightness against the solver where it converges.}
On the subset of cases for which Layer~1--5 do not flag the
solver output, the EMT estimate agrees with the spsolve result to
within $\pm 3\%$, so the fallback is not a degraded approximation
but a numerically-stable substitute that matches the converged
solver where both are available. The combination of bound
preservation and classical-EMT pedigree is what allows us to
report Stage~E values on every one of the 82 cases without
opportunistically dropping the ones that defeat
\texttt{spsolve}.

It is worth noting that the same qualitative pattern --- Bruggeman
over-estimating the SE conductivity by a factor of $\sim 3$ at
relevant compositions --- was independently reported by
\citet{So2021} from their explicit-plastic-flow DEM simulation of
the LPS/Si system, who proposed a modified Bruggeman relation with
a critical SE volume fraction $\varphi_{\mathrm{SE}}^{\mathrm{crit}}
\approx 0.13$ below which the conductivity goes to zero.  This is a
distinct percolation concept from the stress-bearing
$f_{\mathrm{perc}} = 0.65$ of \citet{LiuYin2025} used in
Section~\ref{sec:two-mechanisms}: the former describes geometric
SE--SE connectivity (below which the SE network is electrically
disconnected), the latter describes the SE force-chain participation
ratio (below which SE no longer carries the compaction load).  The
two thresholds are complementary rather than redundant.

\subsection{Sensitivity of the porosity wave-shape}
\label{sec:sensitivity}
The shape of the strict-physics curve in
Figure~\ref{fig:porosity-validation} depends on two literature
constants: $\alpha_{KC} = 2.0$ from \citet{Sridhar2000} and the
SE stress-bearing percolation threshold $f_{\mathrm{perc}} = 0.65$
from \citet{LiuYin2025}. Neither is fitted to our data, but a
reviewer is right to ask how much the wave-shape leans on either
choice. A one-at-a-time sensitivity sweep over the 82-case
ensemble gives the following ranges:

  \begin{itemize}
  \item $\alpha_{KC} \in [1.5, 2.5]$ ($\pm 25$~\%):
        ensemble RMSE varies by $\pm 0.5$~\%-points.  The hump
        height moves by $\le 1$~\%-point.
  \item $f_{\mathrm{perc}} \in [0.55, 0.75]$ ($\pm 15$~\%):
        hump position shifts by $\pm 5$~AM-wt\% (the position
        on the abscissa, not a porosity offset); ensemble RMSE
        varies by $< 1$~\%-point of $\varepsilon$.
  \end{itemize}

Both parameters are therefore robust at the level we report — the
wave-shape conclusion ("two competing densification mechanisms
generate a non-monotonic curve with a Furnas valley at
$\mathrm{AM}\approx 85$~\%") survives the entire literature-
plausible range of either constant. The
\texttt{scripts/diag\_se\_percolation\_threshold.py} diagnostic
described in Section~\ref{sec:future} replaces the
$f_{\mathrm{perc}} = 0.65$ \emph{assumption} with a directly
measured value from our own SE--SE contact networks, completing
the literature-to-measured upgrade for that anchor.

\subsection{Stress-bearing percolation in the bimodal cathode
            regime}
\label{sec:bimodal-perc}
Running the diagnostic of Section~\ref{sec:sensitivity} on the
134-case ensemble and stratifying by campaign reveals that the
$f_{\mathrm{perc}}$ anchor imported from \citet{LiuYin2025} is
operationally relevant only at the mono-AM extreme of our design
space:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Mono-AM (\texttt{particulate}, $n = 20$).}
      Stress-bearing SE fraction drops below the operational
      $\tau = 0.5$ threshold at $\mathrm{AM}_{\mathrm{wt}}^{*} =
      62.16\,\%$, which corresponds to $f_{\mathrm{SE}}^{\mathrm{(i)}}
      = 0.594$ (solid-only convention) or
      $f_{\mathrm{SE}}^{\mathrm{(ii)}} = 0.556$ (RVE-aware
      convention).  Bootstrap 95\,\% CI on
      $f_{\mathrm{SE}}^{\mathrm{(i)}}$ is $[0.546,\,0.594]$ and
      excludes the literature value $0.65$.  The
      $\Delta = -0.06$ to $-0.09$ offset is statistically
      significant but small, and can be attributed to one or more
      of: (a) discrete contact-network vs continuum yield-stress
      mapping, (b) different SE chemistry (our argyrodite vs Liu
      \& Yin's sulfide), (c) ambiguity in the volume-fraction
      convention used by \citet{LiuYin2025} (their Methods section
      should be consulted to resolve (i) vs (ii); the qualitative
      conclusion is invariant under either).
\item \textbf{Bimodal cathodes (\texttt{thin-film 1\,mAh} $n = 35$,
      \texttt{thick-film 6\,mAh} $n = 14$, \texttt{thick-film
      8\,mAh} $n = 17$).}  The stress-bearing SE fraction stays
      \emph{above} $0.5$ throughout the entire studied
      AM$_{\mathrm{wt}}$ range (50--95\,\%) in every one of these
      66 cases.  The strong-network test of
      \citet{Radjai1996}\,---\,which we apply with the standard
      cutoff $|F_n| > \langle |F_n| \rangle$ that separates the
      load-bearing chains from the percolating weak network
      \citep{Mueth1998, Majmudar2005}\,---\,never breaks in bimodal
      data: the operational threshold simply does not cross.
      Extrapolation beyond AM$_{\mathrm{wt}} > 95\,\%$ is not
      validated here.
\end{itemize}

The interpretation is geometric.  Three particle scales
($D_{\mathrm{AM_P}} \approx 6\,\si{\micro\metre}$,
 $D_{\mathrm{AM_S}} \approx 2\,\si{\micro\metre}$,
 $D_{\mathrm{SE}} \approx 0.5\,\si{\micro\metre}$) populate a
hierarchical Furnas-valley packing in which AM$_S$ partially fills
the AM$_P$ voids and SE further fills the residual interstices.
The empirical observation is that this hierarchy preserves
SE-mediated load paths throughout the cathode-relevant
AM$_{\mathrm{wt}}$ range, so the mono-AM-calibrated
$f_{\mathrm{perc}} = 0.65$ value of \citet{LiuYin2025} acts as a
\emph{conservative} anchor for our bimodal regime: it would
predict percolation breakdown earlier than the DEM data shows.

This finding is a \emph{scope clarification} for the strict-physics
porosity model rather than a parameter revision.  The
$\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{plastic}}(\mathrm{AM}) \cdot
p_{\mathrm{se}}(f_{\mathrm{SE}};\,f_{\mathrm{perc}})$ term in
Section~\ref{sec:results-porosity} carries a $p_{\mathrm{se}}
\approx 1$ inside the bimodal regime of
Figure~\ref{fig:porosity-validation}'s panels~\textcircled{1}--%
\textcircled{3}, so the $f_{\mathrm{perc}}$ choice does not
quantitatively shift those predictions.  The hump in the
porosity wave-shape therefore arises from the smooth interplay of
$\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Bouvard}}$ and $\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm
{plastic}}$ across composition; the $f_{\mathrm{perc}}$ gate is a
modulation that matters only at the mono-AM panel~\textcircled{4}
extreme, which our model already labels out-of-regime.  The
wave-shape conclusion therefore does \emph{not} rest on the
specific $0.65$ value within the regime that matters for cathode
design.

\subsection{Future work}
\label{sec:future}
Three concrete extensions remain open. (a) \textbf{Yu--Standish
1996 multimodal RCP} would replace the Bouvard binary
interpolation with a fully trimodal $\{AM_P, AM_S, SE\}$ packing,
addressing panels~\textcircled{2} and~\textcircled{4}; a scaffold
implementation is included as
\texttt{scripts/predict\_porosity\_yu\_standish.py} but the simple
max/min trial-selection variant of the 1991 paper does not
reproduce the binary Furnas valley, motivating a future
smooth-weighted-trial revisit. (b) \textbf{Thin-film wall-effect
corrections} (Westman--Hugill modification of Bouvard) would
quantitatively explain the panel~\textcircled{3} scatter rather
than just accept it as geometry-affected. (c) \textbf{MPM/PFEM
brittle-fracture modelling} of the AM-side material response
would replace the per-contact Lawn-stage classification with
field-resolved crack propagation, removing the empirical
$f_r$ multiplier ladder in favour of a first-principles fracture
energy budget. These items are documented as deferred future
work in
\texttt{docs/Reviewer\_Defence\_Notes.md} and
\texttt{docs/porosity\_wave\_shape\_physics.md}.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
% =====================================================================

We presented a literature-grounded, fracture-aware multi-physics
network solver for ASSB composite cathodes that propagates DEM
particle-scale information all the way to cell-level ASR. The 7-layer
defence with Bruggeman EMT fallback ensures that $\sim$20\,\% of
cases that would otherwise produce non-physical solver outputs are
gracefully recovered while preserving the $f_r \le 1$ constraint.
A 160-case ensemble yields a Pearson $+0.967$ design rule against
AM\_P-dominant compositions and case-level ASR consistent with
recent literature.  On the geometric side, a strict physics-first
porosity predictor with a single experimental anchor reproduces 82
DEM cases at $\pm 5\%$ in 100\,\% of the model-applicable regime
($\sigma < 1\%$), the deviations of the out-of-regime cases tracing
cleanly to documented physical extensions (low-$\lambda$ Bouvard,
mono-AM, wall confinement) that are reserved for principled future
work. Together, the two prediction layers --- network-solver
transport and strict-physics porosity --- establish a transparent,
overfitting-free benchmark against which microstructural design
choices for ASSB cathodes can be evaluated quantitatively.
